title: Wring two gauge blocks crossed, then turned into line
instruction: Wring the 25 mm gauge block onto the top face of the 50 mm block so the two make one stack with their faces in line, then let go of both.
context: Why: gauge blocks carry traceable length to the micrometers, calipers, height gauges and comparators that shops, inspection rooms and calibration labs check parts with, and a size is built by wringing blocks into one stack; a stack that is only set together reads long. The maker's quick guide for thick blocks: cross the blocks at 90 deg in the middle of the measuring faces, rotate them while applying slight force, then align the measuring faces. Set one block squarely on the other and it only rests there: the oil film is never worked out and the top block lifts off alone, yet the stack looks done. The hard part is physical: keeping two 9 mm wide faces flat in contact under a light, straight-down press through a compliant arm for a 90 deg turn about the faces' middle. The other hand may steady the tall 50 mm block while the top block is set down, then lets go for the pressed turn. Done by: quality inspectors, machinists and calibration technicians.
setup: Positions from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left), heights above the table. A bench platform scale (31.5 cm square platform, 12 mm thick, 30 kg capacity, 1 g resolution, tared with the plate and both blocks on it) centred at x 26 cm, y 0, its display filmed beside the blocks; on it a black granite surface plate (grade B, 12 x 12 x 3 in class), 30.5 cm square and 7.6 cm thick, about 21 kg, its top 8.8 cm up. On it, each standing free on a measuring face: a Mitutoyo rectangular steel gauge block, 50 mm nominal, grade 2 (workshop grade, kept for practice), section 35 mm wide and 9 mm thick, 124 g, at x 25 cm, y -2 cm, its 35 mm side along x; and a 25 mm Mitutoyo rectangular steel gauge block of the same grade and section, 62 g, at x 25 cm, y -12 cm, its 35 mm side along y. Oiled faces: before each trial the 50 mm block's upper measuring face and the 25 mm block's lower measuring face (the one it stands on) are wiped with a lint-free cloth moistened with isopropyl alcohol, given a trace of light anti-rust gauge-block oil and wiped almost dry. The 50 mm block's lower face, the 25 mm block's upper face, the plate and the gripper pads stay clean and dry. Both arms start in their ready pose; either hand may steady the 50 mm block, but the turn counts only with no hand on it, the plate or the scale (see scoring). The 25 mm block is to go onto the 50 mm block's top measuring face; the 50 mm block's lower face stays on the plate.
scoring: Measured at the end with a steel rule, a protractor and the trial video, plus a lift test by hand. Wrung: in the simulator, the 25 mm block was gripped (both pads of one gripper within 3 mm of the 25 mm block, closed to under 37 mm apart) and turned a net at least 60 deg (turning back subtracts) in one unbroken spell of being gripped with its lower face touching the 50 mm block's top face (no gap over 0.05 mm at their closest point and tilt under 1.5 deg, so the press goes face to face) and pressed onto it with at least 3 N, read on the bench scale under the plate, while no gripper is within 5 mm of the 50 mm block, the plate or the scale (so that load comes only through the faces), about a point within 6 mm of the face's middle, and has not since been lifted more than 1 mm off the face or slid more than 20 mm off its centre. On a real bench wrung needs both: the video shows that turn (the 25 mm block's turn relative to the 50 mm block, if that one turns with it) made with the scale reading at least 0.31 kg above its tare and no hand or arm on the 50 mm block, the plate or the scale, and after the end photo, lifting the 25 mm block 20 mm straight up by hand, held by its 35 mm ends, lifts the 50 mm block with it. In line: the two blocks' centres within 3 mm across both axes and their long sides within 4 deg. On the face: the 25 mm block's lower face within 1 mm of the 50 mm block's top face, centres within 20 mm of the 50 mm block's face centre, tilted under 3 deg. Released and still: no gripper within 30 mm of either block, and neither block moving more than 1 mm over the last 1 s. Score 0 if at any time, even if put back, a block falls over (tilts more than 30 deg) or drops off the surface plate (a dropped gauge block is nicked), or the 50 mm block is lifted more than 5 mm off the plate. Otherwise the first that fits. 1.0: wrung, in line, released and still. 0.75: wrung and in line but still held or not yet still. 0.5: wrung but not in line. 0.25: the 25 mm block on the face but not wrung. 0: anything else, including the untouched start.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Slide the 25 mm block off the 50 mm one lengthwise (never pull wrung blocks straight apart), wipe the two measuring faces that meet with a lint-free cloth and isopropyl alcohol, apply a trace of gauge-block oil to just those two and wipe it almost off, keep oil off the gripper pads, and stand both blocks on their marked places on the plate (50 mm block at x 25 cm, y -2 cm, 35 mm side along x; 25 mm block at x 25 cm, y -12 cm, 35 mm side along y). Check the plate is on its marks. Run the simulator with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: Rigid bodies; the oil film's hold and drag are not simulated. Wringing is credited from the work: gripped, faces touching (closest point within 0.05 mm, under 1.5 deg: rigid pads let the block rock that much), at least 3 N on the bench scale with no gripper near anything else it carries, a net 60 deg turn. Mitutoyo gives only 'slight force'; 3 N (5x the block's weight) is the floor, as above about 6 N the pinched block pivots in the pads. Scale 20 kN/m, tared. Friction: blocks 0.3, plate 0.5.
